key_insight: The paper argues that LoRA adapters should be treated as information to read from, not as parameters to write into when composing multiple skills. This framing helps explain why naive adapter merging causes interference and points to safer ways to combine task-specific knowledge.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of combining multiple independently trained LoRA adapters into a single model without destructive interference, expensive retraining, or relying on separate adapter routing at inference time.
method: Analyze why common composition methods fail by identifying two implicit design choices made during LoRA merging.
Show that each LoRA update has infinitely many equivalent factorized forms, so the choice of factorization affects how adapters interfere when combined.
Propose a composition perspective that avoids directly writing new information into shared LoRA parameters, instead preserving adapter knowledge in a read-only style.
impact: This matters because it could make multi-skill fine-tuning more reliable, efficient, and scalable for large language models. Practitioners may be able to combine task expertise without costly retraining or losing performance through merge conflicts.

paper_title: New LoRA Skills Should Read but Never Write
